title: Phases, Spots and Trouble
summary: Galileo kept looking, and the sky kept surprising him: Venus grew and shrank like a little Moon, the Sun had dark spots, and Saturn seemed to have ears. His discoveries showed that the Earth goes around the Sun, but some powerful people did not want to hear it, and Galileo spent his last years stuck at home.

sections.heading: Venus Puts On a Moon Costume
paragraphs: In the autumn of 1610 Galileo Galilei was busier and more famous than he had ever been. His little book The Starry Messenger had made him a celebrity across Europe, and that summer he had left his teaching job in Padua to become Chief Mathematician and Philosopher to Cosimo II de' Medici, the Grand Duke of Tuscany, in Florence. No more lectures to bored students. Now he could spend his nights doing what he loved most: pointing his best telescope, about 20 times magnification, at anything bright enough to catch.

One of the brightest things in the evening sky that autumn was Venus. To the naked eye, Venus is a dazzling white dot, so bright that people sometimes mistake it for an airplane's landing light. Through Galileo's tube it was a small disk. But week after week, starting around September 1610 and continuing to the end of the year, he watched that disk do something remarkable. At first it looked almost round, like a tiny full Moon. Then it grew larger and, at the same time, lost part of its light, becoming a half-circle like a quarter Moon. Later still it became a big, thin crescent, like a fingernail clipping of light.

In other words, Venus has phases, just as our Moon does. And it changes size dramatically while doing so. Modern measurements show that Venus looks about seven times wider when it is a thin crescent near Earth than when it is a small, nearly full disk on the far side of the Sun.

Why was this such a big deal? Think back to the old Earth-centered system of Ptolemy, which most scholars still used in 1610. In Ptolemy's arrangement, Venus always stayed between the Earth and the Sun, riding on its own little circle. A planet that stays on the near side of the Sun would always have its sunny side facing mostly away from us. We would see it as a crescent or a thin sliver, never anything close to full. But Galileo saw Venus nearly full. The only way that can happen is if Venus sometimes goes around to the far side of the Sun, so that its whole sunlit face points toward us. That means Venus circles the Sun.

This was the first direct, observed proof that at least one planet orbits the Sun rather than the Earth. It did not prove every part of Copernicus's idea. A clever compromise invented by Tycho Brahe, in which the planets circle the Sun while the Sun circles a motionless Earth, could also explain the phases of Venus. But the classic Ptolemaic system, the standard picture of the heavens for more than 1,400 years, was now in serious trouble.

Galileo was worried someone else might announce the discovery first. In December 1610 he did something sneaky that scientists of his time often did: he sent a scrambled sentence, an anagram, to Kepler by way of the Tuscan ambassador in Prague. The jumbled Latin letters read, roughly, 'These unripe things are now read by me in vain.' A few weeks later he revealed the unscrambled message: 'Cynthiae figuras aemulatur mater amorum,' which means 'The mother of love imitates the shapes of Cynthia.' The mother of love was Venus, the goddess of love, and Cynthia was a poetic name for the Moon. In a single coded line, Galileo had claimed the discovery and kept it secret at the same time.

Was Galileo really first? Historians have noticed that his former student Benedetto Castelli wrote to him in December 1610 asking whether Venus might show phases through a telescope. Whether Castelli was giving Galileo the idea or responding to news Galileo had already shared is still debated. What is certain is that Galileo made the observations carefully, understood what they meant, and published them in 1613.

sections.heading: Spots on the Perfect Sun
paragraphs: For about 2,000 years, many European scholars followed the Greek philosopher Aristotle, who taught that everything above the Moon was perfect, eternal and unchanging. The Sun, in this view, was a flawless ball of heavenly fire. Galileo had already shown that the Moon was rough and mountainous. Now the Sun itself was about to get messy.

Dark spots on the Sun had actually been seen long before telescopes. Chinese astronomers recorded them with the naked eye more than 2,000 years ago, when haze or a low sunset dimmed the glare enough to make a big spot visible. But in Europe such reports were usually explained away, for example as a planet passing in front of the Sun.

Once telescopes appeared, several people spotted sunspots within a few months of each other. The English scientist Thomas Harriot sketched them in December 1610 but never published his drawings. In Germany, a young man named Johannes Fabricius, working with his father David, saw them in early 1611 and printed the first published description that same year. Galileo said he had been watching sunspots since 1610 and showing them to visitors.

Then came Christoph Scheiner, a Jesuit priest and mathematics professor at the university in Ingolstadt, Bavaria. In 1611 Scheiner and his student Johann Baptist Cysat studied the spots carefully. Because Jesuits were cautious about publishing controversial ideas, Scheiner wrote three letters about them to a wealthy Augsburg merchant and scholar named Mark Welser, signing them with a pen name: 'Apelles,' after a famous painter of ancient Greece who supposedly hid behind his paintings to hear what people said about them. Welser had the letters printed in January 1612.

Scheiner's explanation tried to protect the perfect Sun. He suggested the spots were not on the Sun at all, but were swarms of small dark bodies, perhaps tiny planets or moons, circling close to it and passing in front of its face.

Galileo strongly disagreed. Welser sent him the Apelles letters, and Galileo answered with three long letters of his own, which the Accademia dei Lincei, a scientific society in Rome that had made him a member, published in 1613 as Letters on Sunspots. Galileo's arguments were clever. He pointed out that spots near the edge of the Sun look squashed and thin, while the same spots look wider in the middle of the disk. That is exactly what you would expect from markings on the surface of a turning ball, the same way a picture printed on a basketball looks squeezed when it rotates toward the edge. Spots also changed shape, merged, split, appeared and vanished. They behaved like clouds or stains on the Sun, not like solid little planets. And they all moved across the face together, which showed the Sun itself was spinning, about once a month.

Galileo also had a better way to see them. Instead of squinting at the Sun, his circle used a method credited to Castelli: aim the telescope at the Sun and let the image fall on a sheet of white paper held behind the eyepiece. The spots could then be traced with a pen. The book's 38 detailed engravings of the Sun made the spots look strikingly real.

The argument turned personal. Galileo hinted that he deserved credit for seeing the spots first, and Scheiner felt insulted. The quarrel lasted for years. To be fair to Scheiner, he became one of the finest sunspot observers of his century. In his huge book Rosa Ursina, printed between 1626 and 1630, he published detailed observations, described his own instruments for projecting the Sun, and measured the Sun's rotation at about 27 days. By then he had accepted that the spots really were on the Sun. Today we know sunspots are cooler, darker patches where tangled magnetic fields stop some heat from rising to the surface. Each one can be bigger than the whole Earth.

sections.heading: Safety Box: Never Look at the Sun Through a Telescope
paragraphs: Before we go any further, here is the most important rule in this whole Deep Dive. Never, ever look at the Sun through a telescope, binoculars, a camera viewfinder or any other magnifying device unless it has a proper, certified solar filter fitted securely over the front end, the end that faces the Sun.

Here is why. A telescope's whole job is to collect light and squeeze it together. A small backyard telescope might collect hundreds of times more light than your eye. When it is pointed at a dim galaxy, that is wonderful. When it is pointed at the Sun, it focuses an enormous amount of light and heat into one tiny spot, like a magnifying glass burning a leaf. The retina at the back of your eye has no pain nerves, so it can be badly and permanently damaged in a fraction of a second before you even feel anything.

Ordinary sunglasses are not safe for looking at the Sun, not even several pairs at once. Eclipse glasses that meet the international safety standard called ISO 12312-2 are safe for looking at the Sun with your bare eyes, but NASA warns that they must never be used together with binoculars, telescopes or cameras, because the concentrated light can burn straight through them. Optical instruments need their own special filters made for solar viewing, mounted on the front, and it is wise to ask an experienced astronomer to help.

The safest easy way to watch the Sun is the way Galileo's circle traced sunspots: projection. You can poke a tiny hole in an index card, stand with your back to the Sun, and let sunlight through the hole form a small image of the Sun on another card or on the ground. During a partial eclipse, that little image even shows the Moon taking a bite out of the Sun. Just remember: look at the image, never through the hole at the Sun.

sections.heading: The Planet With Ears
paragraphs: In July 1610, before he saw the phases of Venus, Galileo pointed his telescope at Saturn, the slowest and most distant planet known at the time. He expected a simple round disk. Instead, Saturn looked strange, as if it were three objects: a large central ball with a smaller blob stuck tightly on each side. Galileo wrote that Saturn seemed to be made of three bodies that almost touched one another and never moved relative to each other.

Once again he protected his claim with an anagram. He sent out a string of 37 seemingly random letters: smaismrmilmepoetaleumibunenugttauiras. When unscrambled, it read 'Altissimum planetam tergeminum observavi,' meaning 'I have observed the highest planet to be triple.'

Then Saturn played a trick. In late 1612, Galileo looked again and the side blobs had vanished completely. Saturn was a plain, lonely ball. He was baffled and admitted in writing that he did not know what to say about something so surprising and so new.

The blobs came back in 1613. Later Galileo drew Saturn with two curved shapes on its sides like the handles of a sugar bowl or a pair of ears. The 'ears' grew and shrank over the years in a way nobody could explain.

Today we know the answer. Saturn is surrounded by enormous, flat, very thin rings made of countless chunks of ice and rock. They stretch hundreds of thousands of kilometers across but are mostly only about 10 meters to perhaps 1 kilometer thick. Galileo's small telescope could not show the gap between the planet and the rings, so they looked like attached lumps. And because Saturn is tilted, Earth sees the rings from different angles as Saturn travels its 29-year orbit. About every 13 to 15 years, the rings line up exactly edge-on to us. Seen from the side, something that thin almost disappears, which is exactly what happened in 1612.
Galileo never solved the puzzle. It took about 45 more years, a better telescope and a sharp-eyed young Dutchman to figure it out, and that story belongs to the next part.

sections.heading: Believers, Doubters and a Borrowed Telescope
paragraphs: When The Starry Messenger came out in March 1610, many readers were thrilled, but many others were suspicious. Remember, almost nobody else had a telescope as good as Galileo's. Cheap Dutch spyglasses magnified only about three times, which was not enough to see Jupiter's moons clearly. So when Galileo claimed he had found four new worlds circling Jupiter, plenty of scholars wondered whether he was seeing reflections, flaws in the glass, or things that were not there at all.

One of the most famous doubters was Cesare Cremonini, a philosophy professor at Padua and actually a friend and colleague of Galileo's. Cremonini was a devoted follower of Aristotle. According to accounts from the time, when he was invited to look at the Moon's mountains through the telescope, he refused even to put his eye to it, insisting that Aristotle had already shown the Moon must be a perfect sphere. Another Aristotelian professor, Giulio Libri of Pisa, is also said to have refused. Their refusal has become a famous symbol of closing your eyes to evidence, though to be fair, looking through a wobbly early telescope was genuinely tricky, and even people who did look sometimes could not see what Galileo described.

The most important supporter was Johannes Kepler, the Imperial Mathematician to the Holy Roman Emperor in Prague, the same Kepler who had inherited Tycho Brahe's records. Galileo sent him a copy of the book and asked his opinion. Kepler did not yet own a telescope good enough to check, but in April 1610 he published a short, enthusiastic reply called Conversation with the Starry Messenger. He said he trusted Galileo's honesty and began thinking about what the new discoveries might mean.

Kepler still wanted to see for himself. Later in 1610 he borrowed a telescope that Galileo had sent to Duke Ernest of Cologne, a nobleman who was visiting Prague. Over several nights at the end of the summer, Kepler and a few witnesses took turns at the eyepiece. To keep the test honest, each observer is said to have drawn what he saw separately, using chalk on a board, and then they compared their sketches. The tiny points of light beside Jupiter were really there. Kepler quickly published a short report, Narration About Four Wandering Satellites of Jupiter, which was one of the first independent confirmations of Galileo's discovery. It was Kepler who began using the word 'satellite,' from a Latin word for an attendant who follows an important person around, for moons circling a planet.

Support soon came from an unexpected place. The Jesuit astronomers at the Collegio Romano in Rome, led by the respected mathematician Christopher Clavius, managed to get a good telescope and confirmed Jupiter's moons and the phases of Venus. When Galileo visited Rome in the spring of 1611, the Jesuits honored him with a special event, and he was welcomed by cardinals and even Pope Paul V. It was during this visit that he was made a member of the Accademia dei Lincei. Galileo's discoveries were accepted as real. What people would do with them was a different question.

sections.heading: The Warning of 1616
paragraphs: Seeing that Venus circles the Sun was one thing. Saying that the Earth itself moves around the Sun was another. In the early 1600s, many religious leaders read certain lines of the Bible, such as a passage in the Book of Joshua where the Sun is commanded to stand still, as meaning the Sun moves and the Earth stays put. Galileo's growing fame drew attention to Copernicus's idea, and some critics began to say that it contradicted Scripture.

Galileo did not keep quiet. In a letter written in 1613 to his former student Castelli, and then in a much longer letter to the Grand Duke's mother, Christina of Lorraine, in 1615, he argued that the Bible was meant to teach people how to go to heaven, not how the heavens go. If careful observation proved something about nature, he said, then the Bible should be read in a way that fit the facts. At the time, some churchmen thought a mathematician had no business telling theologians how to read Scripture. Copies of the letter to Castelli were sent to the Roman Inquisition, the Church court in charge of fighting heresy, which means beliefs that go against official teaching.

In February 1616 the Inquisition asked a panel of theologians to judge two statements: that the Sun is the motionless center of the world, and that the Earth moves. On 24 February they declared the first one foolish, absurd in philosophy and formally heretical, and the second one at least an error in faith. Two days later, on 26 February 1616, the powerful Cardinal Robert Bellarmine called Galileo in and told him to abandon the Copernican opinion and not to hold or defend it. Exactly what else Galileo was told that day, and whether he was forbidden to discuss the idea in any way at all, became a crucial question many years later, because the surviving records do not completely agree.

On 5 March 1616 the Congregation of the Index, the office that kept a list of forbidden books, suspended Copernicus's On the Revolutions until it was 'corrected.' The corrections, issued a few years later, were mostly small edits that made the Sun-centered system sound like a calculating trick rather than a description of reality. Books arguing that the Earth really moves were banned. Galileo himself was not punished, and he went home to Florence and studied other things for several years.

sections.heading: A Dialogue and a Trial
paragraphs: In 1623 everything seemed to change. A Florentine cardinal named Maffeo Barberini, who admired Galileo and had once written a poem praising him, was elected Pope Urban VIII. Galileo traveled to Rome and met the new pope several times. He came away believing he could write about the Copernican system, as long as he presented it fairly as one possible idea alongside the traditional one, and did not claim it was proven.

He spent years writing a big book called Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems. Instead of a dry textbook in Latin, he wrote it in lively Italian so that ordinary educated readers could enjoy it. It takes the form of a conversation over four days among three friends: Salviati, a brilliant scientist who argues for Copernicus; Sagredo, an intelligent, open-minded nobleman; and Simplicio, a loyal follower of Aristotle and Ptolemy. After getting official permission from Church censors, the book was printed in Florence, and the first copy was presented to Grand Duke Ferdinando II on 22 February 1632.

The trouble was that the book did not feel balanced. Salviati's arguments shine, Sagredo usually agrees with him, and Simplicio, whose name sounds like 'simpleton' in Italian even though it came from an ancient philosopher named Simplicius, often looks silly. Worse, Galileo put one of the pope's own favorite arguments into Simplicio's mouth near the end of the book. Urban VIII was furious and felt betrayed. Within months, sales were stopped and Galileo was ordered to come to Rome.

Galileo was 68, unwell, and begged to be excused, but he had to go. He arrived in Rome in February 1633 and was questioned by the Inquisition from April onward. The key accusation was that he had disobeyed the order given to him in 1616. Galileo claimed his book did not truly defend Copernicus, which was hard to believe for anyone who had read it. In his last questioning he was threatened with torture if he did not tell the truth about his beliefs. This threat was a standard legal step at the time, and historians agree it was not carried out on him.

On 22 June 1633 the court gave its verdict: Galileo was 'vehemently suspected of heresy.' Kneeling in a hall of the convent of Santa Maria sopra Minerva in Rome, dressed in the white robe of a penitent, the old scientist read aloud a statement in which he abjured, which means formally took back, cursed and rejected the idea that the Sun is the center and the Earth moves. The Dialogue was banned, and it stayed on the list of forbidden books until 1835. He was sentenced to prison at the Inquisition's pleasure, but the next day this was changed to house arrest.

You may have heard that as he stood up, Galileo muttered 'Eppur si muove,' 'And yet it moves.' It is a wonderful line, but it is a legend. There is no evidence he said it, and the story first appears in writing more than a century after his death. Saying such a thing in front of the Inquisition would also have been extremely dangerous. Another myth says Galileo was burned at the stake. He was not. The philosopher Giordano Bruno had been burned in Rome in 1600, but for a long list of religious beliefs, not for astronomy alone, and Galileo's punishment was very different.

sections.heading: The Prisoner of Arcetri
paragraphs: Galileo first spent several months in Siena as the guest of his friend Archbishop Ascanio Piccolomini, who treated him kindly and encouraged him to work. Then, at the end of 1633, he was allowed to move to his small country house, called Il Gioiello, which means 'the jewel,' in the hills of Arcetri just outside Florence. He chose it partly to be near the convent where his eldest daughter lived as a nun. Her name was Sister Maria Celeste, and her warm, funny, worried letters to her father still survive. Sadly, she died in April 1634, only months after he arrived, and Galileo was heartbroken.

House arrest meant he could not leave without permission, and visitors were watched. But Galileo did not give up science. He went back to work he had begun decades earlier on how things move and how strong materials are, from falling objects to swinging pendulums to why giant animals need thick bones. The result was his book Two New Sciences. Because his works could not be printed in Catholic Italy, the manuscript was smuggled out and published in 1638 in the Netherlands, the same country where the telescope had first appeared. Many scientists consider it the start of modern physics.

By then Galileo's eyes were failing. He lost sight in one eye and then, around 1638, became completely blind. Doctors today are not sure exactly why. Eye diseases such as cataracts or glaucoma are possible explanations, and there is no good evidence that looking at the Sun was the cause. Yet his mind kept working. Late in life, while blind, he even described a design for a clock controlled by a pendulum to his son Vincenzo, who later tried to build it.

He had some remarkable visitors. Young students came to help him: Vincenzo Viviani, who later wrote his biography, and Evangelista Torricelli, who would soon invent the barometer. The young English poet John Milton later wrote that he had visited the famous Galileo, grown old and a prisoner of the Inquisition.

Galileo died at Arcetri on 8 January 1642, at the age of 77. The Grand Duke wanted to give him a grand tomb, but the pope objected, so he was buried quietly in a side room of the Basilica of Santa Croce in Florence. Only in 1737, nearly a century later, was he moved to a splendid monument in the main church, where visitors can see it today. During that move, a few of his fingers and a tooth were removed by admirers. One of his fingers is still on display at the Museo Galileo in Florence, pointing upward toward the sky.

The story had one more chapter, 350 years later. In 1979 Pope John Paul II asked scholars to study the Galileo case again, and in 1981 a special commission was formed. On 31 October 1992, in a speech to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, the pope acknowledged that the theologians who condemned Galileo had made a mistake, because they had confused the Bible's meaning with one particular way of reading it. By then, of course, spacecraft had flown past every planet Galileo knew, and one of them, NASA's Galileo probe, was on its way to orbit Jupiter and study the very moons he had discovered.

Yet even in Galileo's lifetime, his famous tube was already being left behind. It had a hidden weakness: looking through it was like peering through a keyhole, with a field of view so tiny that only a small part of the Moon fit inside at once. And his correspondent Kepler had already worked out a better design, on paper.

deepDive: Historians now see the Galileo affair as more complicated than a simple fight between science and religion. On the science side, Galileo's telescope evidence was powerful but not complete. The phases of Venus ruled out Ptolemy, yet they fit Tycho Brahe's geo-heliocentric system just as well, and many Jesuit astronomers switched to Tycho's model rather than to Copernicus's. A real proof that the Earth moves needed things nobody could yet measure: stellar parallax, the tiny yearly shift in a nearby star's position, was not detected until 1838, and the aberration of starlight was found by James Bradley in 1729. Galileo's own favorite proof, that Earth's motion causes the tides, was wrong; the Moon's gravity is the main cause, as Kepler had suspected. Galileo also ignored Kepler's discovery that planets move in ellipses, which made the Copernican system far more accurate. On the legal side, the trial turned on an unsigned document in the Inquisition's files saying that in 1616 Galileo had been forbidden to 'hold, teach or defend' the idea 'in any way whatever.' Galileo produced a certificate from Bellarmine that said only that he must not hold or defend it. Scholars still argue whether the stricter note was an accurate record, a misunderstanding, or improperly made. Politics mattered too: Urban VIII was under attack during the Thirty Years' War for being too soft on heresy, and Galileo's apparent mockery came at a bad moment. None of this makes the verdict right; the Church itself said in 1992 that it was a mistake. But it reminds us that big scientific ideas usually win through accumulating evidence, careful argument and time, not a single dramatic moment. Within about 50 years of Galileo's death, Newton's laws of motion and gravity explained why planets orbit the Sun, and by the 1700s educated people across Europe accepted that the Earth moves. Catholic restrictions on Sun-centered books were gradually lifted, with works teaching Earth's motion as physical fact formally allowed by the 1820s, and the Dialogue left the Index in 1835.
funFact: Galileo died in January 1642, and Isaac Newton, who would go on to build the first practical reflecting telescope, was born in England at the end of that same year.

check.q: Why did seeing a nearly full Venus show that Venus goes around the Sun?
check.a: Venus can only look nearly full if it sometimes passes behind the Sun, so it must orbit the Sun
wrong: Because Venus is closer to the stars than Earth is
Because Venus was seen to have its own moons
Because Venus stayed exactly the same size all year
